Biological system of organs and structures used for gas exchange in animals and plants. In land animals the respiratory surface is internalized as the lining of the [[Lung|lungs]], where gas exchange occurs in millions of small air sacs with a rich blood supply: alveoli in [[Mammal|mammals]] and reptiles, atria in [[Bird|birds]]. Airways link these sacs to the environment. The trachea branches in the middle of the chest into two main bronchi, which divide into progressively narrower secondary and tertiary bronchi and then into bronchioles (parabronchi in birds). Air is pumped in by breathing, which involves the muscles of respiration; inhalation at rest results mainly from contraction of the diaphragm.

In humans and other mammals the tract is divided into an upper part (nose, nasal cavities, sinuses, pharynx, and the part of the larynx above the vocal folds) and a lower part (the lower larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli). The branching lower airways, called the respiratory tree, have about 23 generations in the adult human and about 13 in the mouse. Generations 0–16 serve only as conduits; gas exchange takes place in approximately generations 17–23. Because alveoli are dead ends, about 150 ml of dead space stays filled with air after exhalation.

In most [[Fish|fish]] and many other aquatic animals the system consists of [[Gill|gills]], whose thin filaments and lamellae expose a very large surface of vascularized tissue to water. [[Insect|Insects]] have very simple respiratory anatomy, and in [[Amphibian|amphibians]] the skin also plays a vital role in gas exchange. Plants also have respiratory systems, built around [[Stoma|stomata]], but the direction of gas exchange can be opposite to that in animals.

Sale of [[Goods|goods]] and services to consumers, as distinct from wholesaling, which is sale to business or institutional customers. A retailer buys goods in large quantities from manufacturers, directly or through a wholesaler, and sells them in smaller quantities to consumers for a profit, making retailers the final link in the supply chain from producers to consumers. Retail [[Market (economics)|markets]] and shops date back to antiquity; some of the earliest retailers were itinerant peddlers, and over the centuries shops grew from little more than "rude booths" to modern shopping malls.

Retailing often occurs in stores or service establishments but may also take place through direct selling, such as vending machines, door-to-door sales, or electronic channels. The term also applies to service providers that sell to consumers, including retail banking, tourism, insurance, private healthcare, and private education. In some jurisdictions, legal definitions of retail specify that at least 80 percent of sales must be to end-users.

Retail operations center on obtaining goods in needed quantities and placing them where customers will buy them, so purchasing and supply management are core to strategy. Day-to-day decisions are often described through the retail marketing mix of six "Ps": product, place, promotion, price, personnel, and presentation. Pricing tactics include discounts, everyday low pricing, high–low pricing, loss leaders, bundling, and psychological pricing. One cited estimate is that in 2012 about 70% of United States retail workers were part-time. Many retailers have moved to multichannel models combining physical and online sales and have added services such as buy online and pick up in store, while some firms have tested cashierless store formats. Support services may include credit, delivery, and advisory services.

Regulated succession of strong and weak elements, or of opposite or different conditions, in time. The word comes from Greek *rhythmos*, "any regular recurring motion, symmetry." It most commonly refers to such movement of beats in [[Music|music]], but also applies to poetry, mechanical operations, and biological processes, and to cyclical natural phenomena with periodicities from microseconds to many years. The *Oxford English Dictionary* defines rhythm in verse as the measured flow of words or phrases, forming patterns of sound determined by the relation of long and short or stressed and unstressed syllables.

Rhythm is related to, and distinguished from, pulse, meter, and beats. Most music, dance, and oral poetry maintain an underlying metric level, the pulse or beat, a series of identical periodic stimuli to which listeners entrain as they tap a foot or [[Dance|dance]].

In the performing arts, rhythm is the timing of events on a human scale: musical sounds and silences, the steps of a dance, or the meter of speech and poetry. In [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]], the rhythmic delivery of lyrics is one of the most important elements of the style. Rhythm may also be visual, as "timed movement through space"; architects speak of the rhythm of a building in the spacing of windows, columns, and other elements of the [[Façade|façade]]. Percussion, whose fast-transient sounds define a beat clearly, favors cultures that develop polyrhythm and polymeter, as in the cross-rhythms of Sub-Saharan Africa and the interlocking kotekan rhythms of the [[Gamelan|gamelan]].

[[Cereal]] grain, the staple food of over half of the world's population, particularly in [[Africa]] and [[Asia]]. Rice is the seed of the grass species *Oryza sativa* (Asian rice) or, less commonly, *Oryza glaberrima* (African rice). Asian rice was domesticated approximately 13,500 to 8,200 years ago in what is now [[China]]; African rice was domesticated independently in West Africa about 3,000 years ago. In 2023, 800 million tons were produced, third after [[Sugarcane|sugarcane]] and [[Maize|maize]], but only some 8% is traded internationally. China, India, and Indonesia are the largest consumers.

The plant can grow to over 1 m tall, or 5 m in deep water, and takes about six months from seed to harvest. Grain is planted directly in the field, or seedlings are transplanted, as is done by hand for most rice in Asia. Yields are reduced by pests including insects, rodents, and birds, by weeds, and by diseases such as rice blast.

Milling removes the outer layers, giving products from brown rice to white rice. Rice contains no gluten and provides protein but not all essential amino acids; cooked white rice contains 29% carbohydrate and 2% protein, with some manganese. Starch composition determines texture. Long-grain rice from the Indica cultivar is dry and fluffy and includes aromatic varieties such as basmati and jasmine, while short-grain Japonica rice is sticky and used in sushi and mochi. Black rice, colored by [[Anthocyanin|anthocyanins]], was reserved for the royal family in ancient China. Golden rice is a variety [[Genetic engineering|genetically engineered]] to contain vitamin A. Rice production is estimated to have caused over 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2022.

Repeated, structured sequence of actions or behaviors that alters the internal or external state of an individual, group, or environment, regardless of conscious understanding, emotional context, or symbolic meaning. Rituals are a feature of all known human societies and also occur in non-human species, such as elephant mourning or corvid object-leaving. They include the [[Worship|worship]] rites and sacraments of organized [[Religion|religions]] and [[Cult|cults]], rites of passage, atonement and purification rites, oaths of allegiance, coronations, presidential inaugurations, [[Marriage|marriages]], and funerals; even hand-shaking and saying "hello" may be termed rituals. The English word derives from Latin *ritualis*, "that which pertains to rite (*ritus*)," and is first recorded in English in 1570.

Definitions in ritual studies conflict. Kyriakidis describes ritual as an outsider's, or "etic," category for activity that seems irrational or illogical to the observer; an insider, or "emic," performer may use the term to acknowledge that it can look so to the uninitiated. Catherine Bell argues that rituals are characterized by formalism, traditionalism, invariance, rule-governance, sacral symbolism, and performance. [[Eric Hobsbawm]] and Terrence Ranger have argued that many rituals presented as ancient, such as those of the British monarchy, took their actual form in the late nineteenth century.

In [[Psychology|psychology]], ritual is sometimes used in a technical sense for a repetitive behavior used to neutralize or prevent anxiety; it can be a symptom of [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder|obsessive–compulsive disorder]], though such behaviors are generally isolated activities. Some researchers report that rituals regulate emotion, enhance performance under stress, and strengthen group cohesion, and that secular forms, such as athletic pre-game routines or diplomatic protocols, share structural features with religious ones.

Natural stream of fresh water that flows on land or inside caves toward another body of water at a lower elevation, such as an ocean, lake, or another river. A river may run dry before reaching its end or flow only in certain seasons. Rivers are regulated by the [[Water cycle|water cycle]]; water enters them through precipitation, runoff down a slope, melting of glaciers or snow, or seepage from [[Aquifer|aquifers]]. The headwaters are the smaller streams that feed a river, and all land that feeds it makes up its [[Drainage basin|drainage basin]], or watershed, usually separated from others by a ridge. Because groundwater feeds rivers where their elevation is lower than the water table, rivers can keep flowing during drought.

Rivers flow downhill under gravity and merge at confluences, where a tributary joins a larger river. They seldom run straight but [[Meander|meander]]. They carve rock and soil into canyons and valleys by [[Erosion|erosion]] of their beds, and where the flow slows, sediment, or alluvium, forms deltas and islands.

Rivers have sustained human and animal life for millennia, including the first civilizations, and provide food, transportation, drinking water, and recreation. Humans have engineered rivers to prevent flooding, irrigate crops, drive water wheels, and produce hydroelectricity from [[Dam|dams]]. People associate rivers with life and fertility, and with religious, political, social, and mythological meanings. Rivers are threatened by pollution, climate change, and human activity; dams, canals, and levees have eliminated habitats, caused the extinction of some species, and reduced the alluvium carried downstream. Regulation of pollution, dam removal, and sewage treatment have helped improve water quality and restore habitats.

Thoroughfare from one place to another, primarily used for movement of traffic, many of them paved. The words road and street are commonly considered interchangeable, but the distinction matters in [[Urban design|urban design]]: streets serve primarily local access, and stroads combine the features of streets and roads. Types include parkways, avenues, [[Controlled-access highway|controlled-access highways]] (freeways, motorways, and expressways), tollways, local roads, public roads, and private roads. Primary features include lanes, sidewalks (pavement), roadways (carriageways), medians, shoulders, verges, bike paths (cycle paths), and shared-use paths.

Definitions vary. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development ([[OECD]]) defines a road as a line of communication using a stabilized base other than rails or air strips, open to public traffic, primarily for road motor vehicles; this includes bridges, tunnels, junctions, interchanges, and toll roads but not cycle paths. The 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic defines a road as the entire surface of any way or street open to public traffic. In the United Kingdom, the Highways Act 1980 treats a road as any length of highway or other road to which the public has access, including bridges.

Many early roads were simply recognizable routes. By about 10,000 BC human travelers used rough pathways. The world's oldest known paved road was built in Egypt between 2600 and 2200 BC. The Sweet Track, a timber causeway in England built in winter 3807 BC or spring 3806 BC, is one of the oldest engineered roads discovered. In 500 BC, Darius I the Great began an extensive road system for the [[Achaemenid Empire]], including the Royal Road connecting Sardis to [[Susa]]; the system reached as far east as [[Bactria]] and [[India]].

Machine, especially one programmable by computer, capable of automatically carrying out a complex series of actions. A robot may be guided by an external or internal control device. Robots may be humanoid, but most are task-performing machines prioritizing function over aesthetics. They range from humanoids such as Honda's ASIMO to industrial robots, medical operating robots, swarm robots, UAV drones such as the General Atomics MQ-1 Predator, and microscopic nanorobots. [[Robotics]] is the branch of technology dealing with their design, construction, operation, and application. Software agents are usually called bots; an [[Android (robot)|android]] is a humanoid robot, and a [[Cyborg|cyborg]] is a human augmented with artificial machines.

The word comes from the Czech author Karel Capek's play *R.U.R.* (*Rossum's Universal Robots*), from Czech *robota*, "forced labor." Ancient cultures described artificial people: Greek myth included Talos, a bronze man guarding Crete, and the mechanical servants built by [[Hephaestus]]. [[Hero of Alexandria]] created numerous automated devices powered by pneumatics, hydraulics, and steam, and Greek engineers built the [[Antikythera mechanism]], the oldest known analog computer. The first electronic autonomous robots were created by William Grey Walter in [[Bristol]], England, in 1948. George Devol built the first commercial, digital, programmable robot, the Unimate, in 1954; it was sold to [[General Motors]] in 1961 to lift hot metal pieces from die casting machines in New Jersey.

Robots have replaced humans in repetitive and dangerous tasks and in extreme environments such as outer space and the sea bottom. They are blamed for rising technological unemployment, and their use in military combat raises ethical concerns, though studies cited in some accounts report productivity gains in robot-adopting industries.

Naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of minerals or mineraloid matter, also called stone. Rocks are categorized by the [[Mineral|minerals]] included, their chemical composition, and how they formed. They make up the Earth's outer solid layer, the [[Earth's crust|crust]], and most of its interior, except for the liquid outer core and pockets of magma in the asthenosphere. [[Petrology]] studies the character and origin of rocks, and mineralogy their mineral components; the field may extend to planetary geology.

Silicate minerals account for about one-third of all known mineral species and about 95% of the earth's crust. Rocks are grouped into three classes, [[Igneous rock|igneous]], [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary]], and [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic]], and can be transformed from one type to another, as described by the rock cycle.

Igneous rocks form when magma cools in the crust or lava cools at the surface or seabed. Plutonic (intrusive) rocks cool slowly within the crust, as with [[Granite|granite]]; volcanic (extrusive) rocks reach the surface, forming pumice or basalt. Sedimentary rocks form by diagenesis and lithification of sediments produced by the weathering, transport, and deposition of existing rocks, as with limestone and sandstone. Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are transformed by high pressures and temperatures without significant melting, as with marble from limestone or slate from shale.

Humans have used rocks since the earliest times, from Stone Age tools to buildings and infrastructure, and mining extracts rocks and the metals within them. The study of rocks became a formal science in the 19th century; the discovery of radioactive decay in 1896 allowed radiometric dating, and understanding of [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]] developed in the second half of the 20th century.

Genre of popular music that originated in the United States as "rock and roll" in the late 1940s and early 1950s and developed into a range of styles from the late 1950s to the mid-1960s, primarily in the United States and United Kingdom. It drew on the African-American genres of [[Blues|blues]] and rhythm and blues and on country music, with influences from electric blues, folk, and jazz. Rock is typically centered on the [[Electric guitar|electric guitar]], usually in a group with an electric bass guitar, drums, and one or more singers, and is usually song-based, in 4/4 time, with verse–chorus form, though the genre has become extremely diverse.

In the mid-1960s musicians began to advance the album ahead of the single, with [[The Beatles|the Beatles]] at the forefront. In the second half of the 1970s [[Punk rock|punk rock]] reacted with stripped-down, energetic social and political critiques, influencing new wave, post-punk, and alternative rock. Rock was the most popular genre of music in the U.S. and much of the western world from the 1960s up to the 2010s; since then it has lost its position as the pre-eminent popular genre but remains commercially successful, with the influence of [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] and electronic dance music increasingly visible.

Rock has served as a vehicle for subcultures, including greasers, teddy boys and rockers, the hippie movement, which spread from San Francisco in the 1960s, and the goth, punk, and emo subcultures. Inheriting the folk tradition of the [[Protest song|protest song]], it has been associated with political activism and changing attitudes to race, sex, and drug use, and is often seen as an expression of youth revolt against adult conformity.
